extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in culture/late-night comedy; fans of Conan O'Brien and television commentary
extracted.subtask_description: A short-form opinion piece arguing that traditional late-night television is failing, citing changes in audience behavior, costs, and content (politicization vs. escapist comedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Carson-era 'escape' quality
rubrics_metrics.description: "fun, engaging interview that served as an escape and a great way to end the day."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece treats a successful late-night show as one that provides an entertaining, escapist experience for viewers (a relaxing end-of-day ritual), exemplified by old Carson episodes the author fondly recalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid becoming political lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Late-night shows should not turn into political lectures: "they went from being that Carson-esque escape to being political lectures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: hosts 'whining and/or sobbing' about politicians (example cited: Colbert and Kimmel 'whining and/or sobbing at you about how awful Trump is')—this shift alienates audiences according to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production cost / overhead
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows must justify high production costs and staff: "overhead that looked, to me, to be about $600" and "With so many staffers involved, they are expensive to produce."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High fixed costs make traditional late-night vulnerable when audiences shrink; cost-efficiency is presented as a key viability criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reach and platform efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Success is measured by audience numbers achieved relative to cost: "If a guy can do World Series numbers with overhead... and you have every big star lining up... that’s when I profoundly understood that late-night shows are in trouble."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-cost digital formats (e.g., YouTube interview shows like Hot Ones) that draw massive audiences challenge expensive network late-night, implying platforms with better reach-per-dollar are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest desirability / star lineup
rubrics_metrics.description: "every big star lining up to do his show or Chicken Shop Date" signals a show's appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When top talent prefers alternate interview formats, it indicates a shift in what guests and audiences find valuable; guest willingness is a metric of relevance and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'lame bits' and perceived propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hell, I'd say it died the moment Colbert had those dancing vaccines. It was a lame bit, and worse, propaganda."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bits perceived as 'lame' or propagandistic damage a show's credibility and entertainment value; comedic content should avoid overt messaging that feels like persuasion rather than humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean staffing / sustainable production model
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit requirement to reduce expensive staffing levels: "With so many staffers involved, they are expensive to produce."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustainability requires rethinking staffing and production scale so shows can survive with smaller audiences or different revenue models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation in format and business model
rubrics_metrics.description: "someone will figure out a more cost-effective way to produce a quality late-night show."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points to examples (e.g., Gutfeld!, Hot Ones) that suggest new formats or business approaches can sustain late-night-style entertainment; innovation is necessary for future success.
